text.p: Gold continued to shine overnight while base metals markets held generally firm. Oil eased while wheat closed mixed. The CRB Index was down 0.17 at 242.72.
METALS
Base metal markets were flighty during Thursday LME trading, with clear trends difficult to discern, and prices largely finished off their highs after a see-sawing session.

Traders said there was a feeling that some markets like copper and nickel were over-extended and ripe for a solid downside reaction. But with funds picking off price dips, there was little substance to declines.
So, during the session, nickel notched up a new nine-month high, zinc neared its recent two-year peak, while copper and aluminium showed signs of approaching Wednesday's high-points.
However, the lack of follow-through at the highs eventually induced modest retreats.
"At the moment it is the funds that are holding things up -- we are not seeing anything physical," one trader said.

Copper was largely on the defensive, apart from spells of covering which foundered just above $2,400 with producers looking to lock in forward sales. There was also some lending of the spreads, although the premiums mostly held steady. Stocks on Friday are expected to register a decline, some said.
Last Thursday business was at $2,393 a tonne, up just $1 from the previous kerb, but well below the $2,412 peak.
Aluminium probed above the $1,660 level intermittently, but ran into profit-taking and speculative selling. Last trade was at $1,652, a $13 loss from the previous kerb.
Nickel prices flew around in their usual volatile fashion, at one point hitting fresh nine-month highs of $8,180 when buy-stops were triggered above $8,100, traders said.

Underpinning the market are flurries of fund interest, as well as the rumblings from Russia's Norilsk, where strike action is a possibility. But the thinness of the market was accentuated by late action, with prices easing back to close the kerb at $8,070, still up $20.
The zinc market showed signs at one stage of testing the recent two-year peak of $1,235 before prices hurriedly re-traced with copper.
Last business was at $1,227, a $5 gain from Wednesday.
Meanwhile, Swiss commodity trader Glencore continued to strengthen its profile in the market by increasing its stake in France's Metaleurop.
Lead was mostly subdued throughout the session, until late covering helped raise values from overnight levels. By the end of the kerb the market was $10 higher at $675.
GOLD

COMEX April gold up about US$5.00 an ounce at $361.00 in late trading, off its morning high of $364.50 after running into heavy selling from bullion banks, traders said. Earlier a breach of resistance at the January 28 high at $360 set off stop orders, and prompted more fund shortcovering. Spot gold bullion was quoted at $359.35 compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix at $360.00, the highest since January 3, 1997. In New York Wednesday bullion closed quoted $354.00/50.
GRAINS

Wheat closed mixed at 1-3/4 cents a bushel lower to seven cents higher. The market was helped by fund buying centred on new crop July. Floor sources said there were no changes in fundamentals to generate buying, which was seen as a flow on from fund-generated rallies in the soy complex.
OIL

NYMEX crude remained weaker late session Thursday as firmer gasoline prices failed to offset a decline in heating oil and kept crude in price range set Wednesday. "We've hit support, and we should have an inside day today," said a chartist in Chicago of crude. April crude was off 26 cents a barrel at $20.85.
SUGAR

CSCE world sugar futures settled a quiet session unchanged as trade buying in the spot month drove a wedge in the nearby spread, dealers said. Spot March closed at a 0.16 cent premium to benchmark May, compared with a 0.01 cent premium after the previous close. Traders cited short-covering from Far Eastern houses and speculative rolling of March contracts into May. Steady trade and producer scale-up selling beginning at 10.90 cents in May limited gains, they added.
